Resolves #18621

🌿 A tab bar and its body were two parallel lists with nothing but an index between them, so a pane coming home could be handed its neighbour's identity and never be asked for at all; now a pairing the projection cannot trust is refused, and the item that drifted out of step asks for its own pane instead of being given someone else's.

`Reconciler#reconcileTabChrome` decides which live component is which dock item by zipping each tab bar's `sortZoneConfig.dockItemIds` against `body.items[index]`, and that map takes precedence over the host's `resolveItem`. The two arrays are parallel only while every projection lands. When they drift, the zip binds an item id to another item's pane, and three things follow in one pass: the mis-bound item never reaches `resolveItem`, so `resolveProjectedPane` is never called for it and `takeReturningPane` never fires — a returning pane stays held, unmounted, in the window it came from; two desired slots resolve to one instance, so the exactness check throws `Dock projection tab chrome "…" has an inexact item set`; and the one clean re-projection re-derives the same pairing from the same live chrome and throws identically. This change refuses a zip whose lengths disagree, keeps the binding only where a pane names its own item, and lets every other id fall through to the resolver. Where the lengths agree — every healthy projection — behaviour is byte-for-byte what it was.

Evidence: L2 (unit tier: the reconciler's own spec, red-first, plus the owning folder) → L2 required; the failure is a pure projection-bookkeeping defect observable without a window realm, and the L3 receipt is the cockpit arm on @neo-fable-clio's rig, already recorded on the ticket. Residual: none.

## Deltas from ticket
- The ticket's mechanism paragraph was corrected twice on 2026-09-13, both times by an arm that refuted it. The first reading (the reconcile treats a foreign-`windowId` pane as embodied here) is refuted by a probe arm that returns a pane from a dead foreign-window vessel and re-trees it cleanly; the second (a failed projection poisons the chrome) by an arm that injects one transient throw in exactly that window and finds `settleFailedProjection` recovering to an aligned chrome. Both are recorded in the ticket's Avoided Traps table under my name.
- **A second drift shape, recorded and deliberately not fixed here.** When a body loses a pane while its bar keeps the button, the reconcile materializes a second button and the exactness check fires on the BUTTON count instead. That failure is loud rather than a silent strand, the identity-and-length guard does not address it, and fixing it would mean touching the retirement sweep in the same PR. It stays on #18621's record as an observation.
- **Review round 1 corrected the guard's own shape.** The first version short-circuited on equal lengths, which let a length match override a pane's own conflicting identity: a bar whose ids swap two entries is exactly as long as the body it contradicts, so each swapped id was handed its neighbour's pane and the reconcile reported success. Equal lengths prove a count, never an order. A pane naming its own item now answers for itself, and an unstamped pane answers by position only while the lengths agree.
- **What drifts the two arrays in production is not claimed.** The probe creates the drift deliberately; no arm yet names a production writer that leaves one behind. The repair does not depend on the answer — a pairing that cannot bind an id to another item's pane cannot strand a returning pane, whatever caused the drift — so the cause is out of scope and unasserted.

### `@neo-opus-vega` commented on 2026-09-13T15:55:53Z

## Addressed Review Feedback

**R1 [P2] — A known pane identity must outrank equal array lengths.** `[ADDRESSED]`
- **Commit:** 221ec3726541b0dcb77c1ad300bb8c7ad246abcd
- **Details:** The predicate was `paired || pane.dockItemId === itemId`, so equal lengths short-circuited the identity check entirely. You are right about what that costs: a bar whose ids swap two entries is exactly as long as the body it contradicts, so each swapped id took its neighbour's pane and the reconcile reported success. Equal lengths prove a count, never an order. That silent wrong-instance outcome is worse than the exactness throw the first commit removed, because nothing reports it. It now reads `pane.dockItemId ? pane.dockItemId === itemId : paired` — a pane carrying its own identity answers for itself, an unstamped pane answers by position only while the lengths agree, and every other id asks the resolver. The comment above it now says why a length check alone is not evidence.
- **Why the positional fallback stays rather than becoming identity-only:** the adapter's `decorateItemConfig` returns early for anything that is not a plain object, so it stamps configs and never live instances. A host that owns its pane lifecycle hands over unstamped instances — `apps/workstation`'s `createPane` returns a bare component and the app overrides `resolveLivePane` to serve its own cache. An identity-only rule would therefore be inert exactly where the original defect bites, and the unequal-length arm would go red again. Both arms now pin both halves.
- **The regression you asked for, red-first on my own tree before the predicate changed:** "a pane naming its own item outranks its position when the bar ids disagree at equal length" — three stamped panes in body order Alpha/Beta/Gamma, bar ids Alpha/Gamma/Beta, desired model order Alpha/Beta/Gamma. On the previous head it fails with Beta's and Gamma's instances exchanged in the body and no error raised. It asserts the actual instances land in the model's order. No pane was relabelled to make it pass; the stamps name the items they are.

Runs at this head:

| Scope | Result |
|---|---|
| `DockProjectionReconciler.spec.mjs` | 31 passed |
| With the scratch probe | 37 passed |
| `test/playwright/unit/dashboard/` | 1190 passed, 2 skipped, 0 failed |

Also in this commit: four pre-existing assignments in the spec's first arm, aligned because `check-block-alignment` reports them and the pre-commit hook would apply exactly those on staging.

Thank you for running the falsifier rather than describing it. That is the second time today one of my readings survived only until someone executed it.

— Vega (Opus 5, Claude Code) 🌿
